The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$
be real-valued, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval containing $f(x)$ for
almost every $x$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$ be convex with
$\varphi\circ f\in L^1(\mathbb P)$. Then
$$\varphi\!\left(\int f\,d\mathbb P\right)\le\int\varphi(f)\,d\mathbb P.$$

For $x>0$, define the **integral logarithm**

$$L(x):=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t},$$

using the oriented integral when $x<1$
([[def-oriented-integral]]).

This is well defined. The function $t\mapsto1/t$ is continuous wherever
$t\neq0$ by the quotient clause of
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. For $x\neq1$ it is therefore continuous on the nondegenerate compact interval
with endpoints $1$ and $x$, hence Riemann integrable there by
[[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], whose hypothesis is $a<b$. At $x=1$ the
interval is degenerate and that theorem does not apply; there
[[def-oriented-integral]] stipulates $\int_1^1f=0$, so $L(1)=0$ directly.

For every $x>0$,

$$L(x)=\log x.$$

For every $x>0$,

$$L'(x)=\frac1x,$$

and $L(1)=0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].
If $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is twice differentiable on an open interval, then $f$ is convex if and only if $f''(x)\ge0$ for every $x\in I$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

A **measure space** is a triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ in which $X$ is a set, $\mathcal A$ is a sigma-algebra on $X$, and $\mu$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measure]]). The members of $\mathcal A$ are the **measurable sets** of the space.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

The **extended real line** is

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}$$

with the total order extending the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$ and satisfying
$-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every real $x$
([[def-extended-reals]]).

Its **Borel sigma-algebra** is the Borel sigma-algebra of that ordered
topological line in the sense of [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]. On this page it is
denoted $\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})$ and is generated by the rays

$$\{\, (a,+\infty] : a \in \mathbb{R} \,\}.$$

In particular, $\{+\infty\}$ and $\{-\infty\}$ are Borel sets.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $f : X \to \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ with $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ as in
[[def-extended-reals]]. Its **positive part** and **negative part** are

$$f^+ := \max\{f,0\},\qquad f^- := \max\{-f,0\}.$$

Pointwise, both functions take values in $[0,+\infty]$, and one has

$$f = f^+ - f^-,\qquad |f| = f^+ + f^-.$$

At each point at least one of $f^+$ and $f^-$ is zero.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$m \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b],$$

with $m, M$ real. Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]), so its Darboux sums
and integrals are defined ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-darboux-integral]]), and
for **every** partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]])

$$m(b-a) \;\le\; L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) \;\le\; M(b-a) .$$

In particular, taking $f$ to be the constant function with value $c$:

$$\int_a^b c \;=\; c\,(b-a) ,$$

the constant function being integrable, with $L(f,P) = U(f,P) = c(b-a)$ for
every partition $P$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: If $P\not\ll Q$, [F1] gives $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$ but $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$, nonnegativity is immediate. It remains to consider $P\ll Q$ with finite divergence; let $r=dP/dQ$.

Put $\varphi(0)=0$ and $\varphi(t)=t\log t$ for $t>0$. By [F5] and [F7], $\varphi''(t)=1/t>0$ for $t>0$, so [F8] makes $\varphi$ convex on $(0,\infty)$. Its continuity at zero is part of [F1]; taking limits in the convexity inequality as a positive endpoint tends to zero extends convexity to $[0,\infty)$.

Define $g(t):=t\log t-t+1$ for $t>0$ and $g(0):=1$. For $s>1$, set $c=(1+s)/2$. By [F11], $\log s=\int_1^cdu/u+\int_c^sdu/u$. On $[1,c]$, $1/u\le1$, while on $[c,s]$, $1/u\le1/c<1$; [F9] and [F24] give $\log s<s-1$. For $0<s<1$, set $c=(1+s)/2$. By [F11], $\log s=-\int_s^1du/u=-\left(\int_s^cdu/u+\int_c^1du/u\right)$. On $[s,c]$, $1/u\ge1/c>1$, and on $[c,1]$, $1/u\ge1$; [F9] and [F24] give $\log s<s-1$. The integrands and comparison constants are integrable on these compact intervals by [F10]. Equality holds at $s=1$. Applying this inequality to $s=1/t$ and using [F6] gives $t\log t\ge t-1$, strictly unless $t=1$. Hence $g\ge0$ and its only zero is $1$.

For the normalized-density clause on the measure space [F13], put $P:=q\,\mu$ and $Q:=\pi\,\mu$. By [F17], $\int\pi\,d\mu=Z^{-1}\int\gamma\,d\mu=1$; hence [F15] and [F14] make $P$ and $Q$ probability measures.

If $Q(E)=0$, [F15] gives $\int_E\pi\,d\mu=0$, hence $\int_E\gamma\,d\mu=0$ because $Z$ is finite and positive, using [F17]. By [F12], $\gamma=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $E$. The support hypothesis on $q$ then gives $P(E)=0$, so $P\ll Q$. Define $\rho:[0,\infty]\to[0,\infty]$ by $\rho(t)=1/t$ for finite $t>0$ and $\rho(0)=\rho(+\infty)=0$. For $a<0$, $\{\rho>a\}=[0,\infty]$; for $a=0$ it is $(0,\infty)$; and for $a>0$ it is $(0,1/a)$. These are Borel by [F18], so [F19] makes $\rho$ Borel. By [F20]–[F21], $r:=q\,\rho(\pi)$ is measurable and equals $q/\pi$ on $\{\pi>0\}$ and zero on $\{\pi=0\}$. For every measurable $E$, [F16] gives $$ \int_E r\,dQ=\int_Er\pi\,d\mu=\int_Eq\,d\mu=P(E), $$ because $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{\pi=0\}$. Thus $r=dP/dQ$.

By [F2] with $E$ equal to the whole space, $\int r\,dQ=P(\Omega)=1$. The negative part of $r\log r$ is finite by [F1], so finiteness of $D(P\|Q)$ also makes its positive part finite. Thus $r$ and $r\log r$ are integrable with respect to the probability measure $Q$. The Radon–Nikodym representative here is the one whose selection is covered by [A1].

On the $P$-full-measure subset of $\{q>0\}$ where $\gamma>0$, we have $\pi=\gamma/Z>0$ and $\ell:=\log r=\log q-\log\gamma+\log Z$. Where $q=0$, the KL logarithm $\ell$ is defined to be zero. By [F23], $q|\ell|\le q|\log q|+q|\log\gamma|+q|\log Z|$ almost everywhere. The right-hand side has finite integral by the hypotheses and $\int q=1$; hence [F16] gives $\int|\ell|\,dP=\int q|\ell|\,d\mu<\infty$. By [F1], [F16], and [F22], applying [F16] to the positive and negative parts of $\ell$ gives $$ D(P\|Q)=\int\log r\,dP =\int q(\log q-\log\gamma+\log Z)\,d\mu. $$ Using $\int q\,d\mu=1$ and rearranging proves the identity.

Apply [F3] on $(\Omega,\mathcal A,Q)$ to $r$ and $\varphi$. Steps 2.1 and 1.2 check its integrability and convexity hypotheses, and $\int r\,dQ=1$ by step 2.1. Therefore $$ 0=\varphi(1)=\varphi\!\left(\int r\,dQ\right) \le\int\varphi(r)\,dQ=D(P\|Q). $$

The representative $r$ is finite-valued and measurable by [F1], and $\varphi(r)$ is measurable there; the arithmetic measurability result [F21] therefore makes $g(r)=\varphi(r)-r+1$ measurable. It is nonnegative by step 1.3. By step 2.1, $r,\varphi(r)\in L^1(Q)$, and $1\in L^1(Q)$ because $Q$ is a probability measure. Linearity [F25] now gives $g(r)\in L^1(Q)$ and $$\int g(r)\,dQ=\int\varphi(r)\,dQ-\int r\,dQ+\int1\,dQ=D(P\|Q)-1+1=D(P\|Q).$$ Thus if $D(P\|Q)=0$, [F12] applies to the measurable nonnegative integrand and gives $g(r)=0$ $Q$-almost everywhere. By step 1.3, $r=1$ $Q$-almost everywhere, and the Radon–Nikodym identity [F2] gives $P(E)=Q(E)$ for every measurable $E$. Conversely, if $P=Q$ then $r=1$ almost everywhere and [F1] gives $D(P\|Q)=0$.
Step 2.2 identifies the normalized-density divergence as finite, and step 3.1 proves it is nonnegative. Therefore $\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu\le\log Z$, as claimed.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, and
$(\mathsf Z,\mathcal C)$ be measurable spaces (sets equipped with
sigma-algebras; [[def-measurable-space]]). Let $\nu$ and $\mu$ be sigma-finite
reference measures on the observation and latent spaces; each has a countable
measurable cover by sets of finite measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). The finite product
sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product
reference measure $\nu\otimes\mu$ is the one supplied by
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]].

A **jointly measurable latent-variable density** is a specified function
$$ p:\Theta\times\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z\longrightarrow[0,\infty] $$
measurable for $\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal C$ and normalized
on every parameter fibre:
$$ \int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\, (\nu\otimes\mu)(d(x,z))=1\qquad(\theta\in\Theta). $$
Here $x$ is the observed coordinate and $z$ the latent coordinate. The
observed marginal density is
$$ m(\theta,x):=\int_{\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz). $$

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

The **extended real line** is

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}$$

with the total order extending the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$ and satisfying
$-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every real $x$
([[def-extended-reals]]).

Its **Borel sigma-algebra** is the Borel sigma-algebra of that ordered
topological line in the sense of [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]. On this page it is
denoted $\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})$ and is generated by the rays

$$\{\, (a,+\infty] : a \in \mathbb{R} \,\}.$$

In particular, $\{+\infty\}$ and $\{-\infty\}$ are Borel sets.

$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be continuously
Fréchet differentiable. The gradient $\nabla f(x)$ is the vector of partial
derivatives in the Euclidean coordinates, with the convention of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; differentiability is the Fréchet
condition of [[def-real-frechet-derivative-on-real-and-complex-matrix-spaces]].

**Inputs:** an initial point $x_0\in U$; either a positive fixed-step
sequence $(t_k)_{k\ge0}$ or backtracking parameters $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and
$\beta\in(0,1)$; and an optional caller stopping predicate
$S(k,x,g)\in\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$, with
$S:\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\times U\times\mathbb R^d\to\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$.
If no predicate is supplied, use $S\equiv\mathrm{false}$. **Output:** when the
procedure stops, return the last valid iterate $x_k$ and the status
`stationary`, `caller-stop`, or `domain-failure`.
If no stopping status occurs, the sequence continues and there is no finite
return.
For example, an outer procedure's at-most-$M$-updates limit, for finite real
$M\ge0$, is implemented by $S(k,x,g):=(k+1>M)$.

At iteration $k$, where $k$ is the number of accepted updates so far and the
current iterate is $x_k$:

1. Compute $g_k:=\nabla f(x_k)$ and set $p_k:=-g_k$. If $g_k=0$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
2. If $S(k,x_k,g_k)$ is true, return $(x_k,\texttt{caller-stop})$. Check this
   predicate at the current iterate after its gradient is computed and before
   any step is selected.
3. In fixed-step mode, set $t=t_k$. If $x_k+tp_k\notin U$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{domain-failure})$ without accepting that candidate.
4. In backtracking mode, start with $t=1$ and repeatedly replace $t$ by
   $\beta t$ until $x_k+tp_k\in U$ and
   $f(x_k+tp_k)\le f(x_k)+\alpha t\,\langle g_k,p_k\rangle$.
5. Set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t p_k$ and continue at iteration $k+1$.

The fixed-step update map is $x\mapsto x-t_k\nabla f(x)$; at a stationary
point its value is $x$, which is the returned iterate. A backtracking search
that is reached at a nonstationary iterate is well-defined by
[[lem-armijo-backtracking-terminates-for-strict-descent-directions]]. The
procedure asserts no convergence or global-minimization property for an
arbitrary objective.

Let $d\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be twice
continuously Fréchet differentiable. Write $g(x)=\nabla f(x)$ and
$H(x)=\nabla^2 f(x)$ using [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and
[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. The Hessian is symmetric by
[[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]].

**Inputs:** $x_0\in U$, a Newton-decrement tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, and
line-search parameters $\alpha\in(0,1/2)$ and $\beta\in(0,1)$. **Output:**
when the procedure stops, return the last valid iterate $x_k$ and one of the
statuses `stationary`, `decrement`, or
`positive-definite solve unavailable`.
If none of these stopping conditions occurs, the sequence continues and there
is no finite return.

At iteration $k$ with current iterate $x_k$:

1. Compute $g_k:=g(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
2. If $H_k:=H(x_k)$ is not positive definite, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{positive-definite solve unavailable})$ without a Newton
   update. Otherwise compute its Cholesky factorization $H_k=L_kL_k^T$, solve
   $L_kw=-g_k$ and $L_k^Tp_k=w$, and set
   $$\lambda_k^2:=-\langle g_k,p_k\rangle=g_k^TH_k^{-1}g_k>0.$$
3. Before line search, if $\lambda_k^2/2\le\varepsilon$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{decrement})$. This is the Newton-decrement stopping test.
4. Start with $t=1$ and repeatedly replace $t$ by $\beta t$ until
   $x_k+t p_k\in U$ and
   $f(x_k+t p_k)\le f(x_k)+\alpha t\,\langle g_k,p_k\rangle$.
5. Set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t p_k$ and continue at iteration $k+1$.

The Cholesky factor exists and is unique when the symmetric Hessian is positive
definite by
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Its positive diagonal makes both triangular solves unique. The backtracking
branch terminates whenever it is reached, since $g_k\ne0$ and $H_k$ is
positive definite, by
[[lem-armijo-backtracking-terminates-for-strict-descent-directions]]. This
procedure makes no global-optimality claim.

Let $U$ be an open subset of a real matrix space $\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ or of
a complex matrix space $\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ viewed as a real vector space,
and let $F:U\to W$ take values in a finite-dimensional real normed vector
space $(W,\|\,\cdot\,\|_W)$.
We say that $F$ is **real Fr\'echet differentiable** at $A\in U$ if there is a
real-linear map $L$ such that

$$\frac{\|F(A+H)-F(A)-L[H]\|_W}{\|H\|_F}\longrightarrow0\qquad(H\to0,\ H\ne0).$$

That map $L$ is the **real Fr\'echet derivative** of $F$ at $A$ and is denoted
$DF(A)$.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]), let
$x \in \mathbb{R}$ with $x \ge -1$, and let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, with powers as in
[[def-integer-power]] and with $n$ also denoting the canonical field image
$n\cdot1_{\mathbb{R}}$ of the natural number n ([[lem-of-naturals-positive]], [[lem-of-q-embeds]]).
Then

$$(1+x)^n \ge 1 + nx,$$

and equality holds if and only if $n \le 1$ or $x = 0$.

for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$ and $\tau>0$. For the normal location
laws with common variance $\tau^2$,
$$D\bigl(N(a,\tau^2)\|N(b,\tau^2)\bigr)=\frac{(a-b)^2}{2\tau^2}.$$

Assume AC and use the directional convention of
[[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. For probability measures $P,Q$ on one
measurable space, $D(P\|Q)\ge0$, and $D(P\|Q)=0$ if and only if $P=Q$.

There is also the following normalized-density identity. Let
$(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space: it is a set
with a sigma-algebra and measure ([[def-measure-space]]), and there is a
countable measurable cover by sets of finite $\mu$-measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). Let
$\gamma:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable function with
$Z:=\int\gamma\,d\mu\in(0,\infty)$, and put $\pi=\gamma/Z$. Let
$q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be a finite-valued measurable probability density,
so $\int q\,d\mu=1$, and suppose $q=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on
$\{\gamma=0\}$. Assume
$$ \int q\bigl(|\log\gamma|+|\log q|\bigr)\,d\mu<\infty, $$
where each term with $q=0$ is defined to be zero. Then
$$ \log Z =\int q(\log\gamma-\log q)\,d\mu +D(q\,\mu\|\pi\,\mu). $$
In particular, the first integral is at most $\log Z$. This identity concerns
normalized densities only; it does not assert posterior existence for an
unspecified statistical model.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, and
$(\mathsf Z,\mathcal C)$ be measurable spaces (sets equipped with
sigma-algebras; [[def-measurable-space]]). Let $\nu$ and $\mu$ be sigma-finite
reference measures on the observation and latent spaces; each has a countable
measurable cover by sets of finite measure
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]). The finite product
sigma-algebra is generated by measurable rectangles
([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]]). The product
reference measure $\nu\otimes\mu$ is the one supplied by
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]].

A **jointly measurable latent-variable density** is a specified function
$$ p:\Theta\times\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z\longrightarrow[0,\infty] $$
measurable for $\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A\otimes\mathcal C$ and normalized
on every parameter fibre:
$$ \int_{\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\, (\nu\otimes\mu)(d(x,z))=1\qquad(\theta\in\Theta). $$
Here $x$ is the observed coordinate and $z$ the latent coordinate. The
observed marginal density is
$$ m(\theta,x):=\int_{\mathsf Z}p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz). $$
The valid-fibre set is
$V:=\{(\theta,x):0<m(\theta,x)<\infty\}$. Only on $V$ define the normalized
latent-fibre density
$$ q(z\mid\theta,x):=\frac{p(\theta,x,z)}{m(\theta,x)}. $$
This definition requires a single jointly measurable density as an input.
[[def-likelihood-density]] supplies neither a sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ nor
joint parameter measurability from separately specified likelihood sections;
the joint measurability above is an additional hypothesis. Because $p$ is
already supplied as one joint function, this definition uses no choice axiom.
It does not assert that AC can turn separately specified pointwise likelihood
versions into a jointly measurable version. No quotient or pointwise
conditional density is asserted on a zero or infinite marginal fibre.

Assume the hypotheses of
[[def-latent-variable-joint-and-observed-data-factorization]]. Then
$m(\theta,x)=\int p(\theta,x,z)\,\mu(dz)$ is jointly measurable in
$(\theta,x)$. For each fixed $\theta$, it is an observed-data probability
density: it is $\mathcal A$-measurable and
$$ \int_{\mathsf X}m(\theta,x)\,\nu(dx)=1. $$
Consequently $m(\theta,x)<\infty$ for $\nu$-almost every $x$. On every valid
fibre $0<m(\theta,x)<\infty$, $q(z\mid\theta,x)=p(\theta,x,z)/m(\theta,x)$ is
a measurable $\mu$-density of total mass one. Finally, if $h:\Theta\times\mathsf X\times\mathsf Z\to\mathbb C$ is product
measurable and
$\int |h(\theta,x,z)|p(\theta,x,z)\,d(\nu\otimes\mu)<\infty$ for a fixed
$\theta$, Fubini permits exchanging the latent and observed integrals of
$hp$. No exchange is claimed without this absolute integrability.

For fixed $A$ and $b$, let

$$f(x):=\frac12\|Ax-b\|_2^2.$$

Then

$$Df(x)[h]=\operatorname{Re}\langle A^\ast(Ax-b),h\rangle,$$

so the gradient is $\nabla f(x)=A^\ast(Ax-b)$ and the Hessian is the constant
map $h\mapsto A^\ast Ah$.

A $C^2$ function on an open convex set is convex if and only if its Hessian is positive semidefinite at every point. Hessians and their quadratic forms have the conventions of [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]], [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]].

Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable and have an
attained minimum $f^*=f(x^*)$. Say that $f$ is $L$-smooth when
$\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y$, and
$\mu$-strongly convex when
$$ f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle +\frac{\mu}{2}\|y-x\|^2 \qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d). $$
If $0<\mu\le L$ and [[alg-gradient-descent]] uses the fixed step $1/L$, then
the initial gap is unchanged at $k=0$, and for every generated iterate $x_k$
with integer $k\ge1$,
$$ f(x_k)-f^*\le \left(1-\frac{\mu}{L}\right)^k\bigl(f(x_0)-f^*\bigr). $$
For $\mu=L$, the factor is zero only for the stated $k\ge1$ range; no
$0^0$ convention is used.

derivations.claim: Take $A=I_d$ in [F1]. Then $\nabla f(x)=x-b$ and $H_f(x)=I_d$. This Hessian is positive semidefinite, so [F2] proves convexity.

Direct expansion gives, for all $x,y$, $$ f(y)=f(x)+\langle x-b,y-x\rangle+\tfrac12\|y-x\|^2. $$ Thus the strong-convexity inequality holds with $\mu=1$. The gradient satisfies $\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|=\|x-y\|\le2\|x-y\|$, so $L=2$ is valid. The minimum is $f^*=0$ at $x=b$.

Whenever the algorithm makes a fixed-step update with step $1/2$, $x_{k+1}=x_k-\tfrac12(x_k-b)=b+\tfrac12(x_k-b)$. Induction along the generated iterates gives $\|x_k-b\|^2=4^{-k}\|x_0-b\|^2$, so $f(x_k)-f^*=4^{-k}(f(x_0)-f^*)\le2^{-k}(f(x_0)-f^*)$ for each generated $k\ge1$; for $k=0$ the gap is unchanged. A caller stop ends this finite prefix and does not assert later iterates. This is the bound from [F3] with $\mu/L=1/2$.
